title: PALM: Point-in-Time Adaptation for Financial Language Models
abstract: Language models used in financial backtests suffer from look-ahead bias, as a model trained on text published after the study period has already observed the outcomes it is asked to predict. To handle this issue, point-in-time (PIT) language models are pretrained on chronologically filtered corpora and released as one checkpoint per calendar year, each with a documented cutoff. However, each additional year costs a full pretraining run, and whether that run is necessary has never been tested. In this paper, we show that the annual pretraining run is not necessary. We instead compare each checkpoint against the newer one that replaced it, and find that the newer checkpoint scores no better on the same evaluation window. Motivated by this observation, we propose PALM (Point-in-time Adaptation for financial Language Models), a simple yet effective alternative to annual pretraining that fits a low-rank adapter on text published before the decision date without modifying any pretrained weight. We further find that a small adapter is enough to add a new period to the knowledge an old checkpoint already encodes, and that this outperforms continued pretraining. We validate PALM on a decade of financial news and on various families of PIT models, whose cutoffs span two decades and whose sizes range from 1.3 to 4.2B. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/palm.

title: Discretization-Aware Fine-Tuning for Quantum Machine Learning with Chemical Foundation Models
abstract: A key challenge in practical quantum machine learning (QML), particularly for discriminative tasks such as classification, is the limited capacity of near-term quantum devices to encode high-dimensional classical data into small quantum registers. In optimized basis-encoded (bit-bit) settings, this constraint leads to cross-class collisions, where samples with different labels are mapped to the same discrete bit-string and thus become indistinguishable to any downstream model. In this work, we investigate how data representation affects QML performance under such severe information bottlenecks. We introduce discretization-aware fine-tuning (DAFT), a method that adapts a pre-trained chemical foundation model to produce representations that remain informative after quantization. DAFT reduces collision probability through a differentiable soft collision loss. We evaluate both quantum and classical models under a controlled setting in which they receive identical discretized bit-string inputs, isolating the effect of representation from model architecture. On the blood-brain barrier penetration (BBBP) molecular property prediction benchmark using ChemBERTa-77M, DAFT reduces collision counts by several orders of magnitude and improves quantum classification accuracy by more than 12 percentage points compared to a frozen backbone. Importantly, without DAFT, classical models outperform QML under the same input constraints. With DAFT, however, this comparison reverses at higher qubit counts. At 10 qubits, the quantum model surpasses a matched classical baseline trained on identical bit-strings (0.883 vs. 0.855, $p = 0.026$). These results show that, in information-constrained regimes, achieving a quantum advantage critically depends on aligning continuous representations with discrete quantum encodings.

title: Stereo 4D Radar for 3D Object Detection: Integrating Geometric Alignment and Absolute Velocity Estimation
abstract: Four-dimensional (4D) Radar is a powerful sensing modality capable of detecting surrounding three-dimensional (3D) objects under diverse weather conditions and providing Doppler-based motion information. However, raw 4D Radar signals contain significant clutter from road surfaces, guardrails, and surrounding vehicles, along with multipath-induced ghost reflections and the receiver's inherent noise floor. Consequently, preprocessing algorithms designed to remove such invalid measurements often make the Radar data excessively sparse. Moreover, the Doppler measurements provided by 4D Radar describe only the radial component of an object's velocity, limiting their ability to recover the full motion state. In this paper, we introduce a stereo 4D Radar-based 3D object detection framework that exploits the geometric disparity between left and right Radars to estimate the absolute velocity of objects and achieve more robust perception through the fusion of their complementary features. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated on our in-house stereo 4D Radar dataset, demonstrating performance gains of 8.82 points in AP 3D and 9.0 points in AP BEV over state-of-the-art mono 4D Radar baselines. These results demonstrate that absolute velocity estimation combined with stereo geometry-aware feature fusion leads to substantial improvements in 3D object detection.

title: Borrowing Knowledge Across Tasks: A State of the Art Review of Transfer Learning and the Pretraining Paradigm
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Transfer Learning and the Pretraining Paradigm in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of transfer learning and pretraining as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: 基于量子自适应的混沌积分算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to chaotic integral computation utilizing a quantum-adapted chaos integral structure. Traditional methods often suffer from limitations in computational efficiency, particularly with high-dimensional integrals. This research explores a new algorithm that leverages the unique properties of quantum self-adapted chaos integrals to enhance performance. The core mechanism involves designing and implementing a quantum-enhanced integral calculation, demonstrating improved efficiency and accuracy compared to established techniques for complex integrals. The proposed method offers a promising avenue for advancing the field of chaos integral analysis, and the potential for significant computational speedups makes it a worthwhile area of investigation.

title: Non-linear Information Encoding
abstract: This paper presents a novel information encoding scheme based on quantum entanglement, aiming to achieve precise information transfer and storage through the manipulation of quantum entanglement. Traditional information encoding methods rely on classical bits, while this approach leverages quantum entanglement for enhanced compression and decryption capabilities. The core mechanism involves constructing an entangled quantum information network, utilizing entanglement's self-adaptative properties to encode and decode information. This design offers potential advantages in terms of efficiency and security. We explore the fundamental principles underpinning this system and detail the experimental setup and analysis.

title: Dynamic Probability Field Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic probability field adaptive optimization algorithm designed to enhance optimization and control processes in machine learning and reinforcement learning. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their adaptability to complex scenarios. This algorithm dynamically adjusts the probability field, allowing the optimization process to self-correct and generalize better. We propose a framework that utilizes the inherent properties of probability distributions to guide the optimization process, leading to improved performance in challenging environments. This work addresses the limitations of traditional optimization techniques by providing a flexible and adaptive solution capable of handling variable data and non-linear relationships. The algorithm's core mechanism involves a probabilistic framework that continuously monitors and adjusts the probability field, optimizing the objective function based on these dynamic adjustments. We explore the benefits of this approach, particularly in scenarios where data is sparse or the objective function is highly non-convex. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance through simulations and experiments, demonstrating its efficacy in several machine learning and reinforcement learning applications.

title: Dynamically Weighted Graph Attention Networks for Adaptive Feature Selection
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to Graph Attention Networks (GATs) that addresses the limitation of fixed attention weights. We propose Dynamically Weighted Graph Attention Networks (DW-GATs) which incorporate a dynamic weighting scheme for attention, allowing the network to adapt to the varying importance of nodes and edges within a graph. The core mechanism involves learning a relevance score for each node based on its features and the graph's connectivity. This relevance score then dynamically influences the attention weights calculated by the GAT layers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DW-GATs in adaptive feature selection, showcasing improved performance compared to traditional GATs, particularly in scenarios with noisy or imbalanced graph data. The proposed method offers a flexible and robust framework for graph representation learning where node importance is not static.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement for Data Compression & Analysis
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers a unique potential for data compression and analysis beyond classical methods. This paper explores the design of a quantum algorithm predicated on leveraging entangled particles to achieve exponential compression. We propose a novel quantum state transfer algorithm centered on identifying and exploiting correlations inherent within entangled states, aiming to significantly reduce computational burden compared to classical approaches. The core mechanism involves meticulously constructing and manipulating quantum states to maximize the fidelity of correlations, ultimately leading to improved data compression rates. The study will detail the algorithm's design, potential challenges, and preliminary results demonstrating enhanced compression capabilities.

title: Title: Bayesian Constraint Optimization for Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian constraint optimization framework designed to address the complexities of solving dynamic systems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the inherent uncertainty present in these systems, leading to suboptimal solutions. Our approach leverages Bayesian methods to model the system's evolution, iteratively refining the optimization process to prioritize stability and resilience to initial conditions. We introduce a novel Bayesian model incorporating both the system's dynamics and the probabilistic uncertainties inherent in the problem. The framework incorporates a probabilistic uncertainty quantification scheme, allowing for a more robust and adaptive optimization process. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through several illustrative examples, showcasing improved performance compared to existing methods in scenarios with significant uncertainty and sensitivity to initial conditions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the framework's strengths, limitations, and potential applications in diverse fields.

title: Nonlinear Topology Models in Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-linear topology models to quantum computing, focusing on the design of quantum circuits leveraging these models to enhance both efficiency and accuracy. We present a novel approach integrating non-linear topology with circuit design, aiming to optimize quantum circuit pathways through the application of these models. The core claim is that a carefully designed system of non-linear topology can significantly improve the performance of quantum computation. The mechanism involves utilizing the model's inherent properties to guide circuit design, leading to increased operational efficiency and reduced error rates. The significance of this research lies in its potential to unlock new possibilities within quantum computing, moving beyond traditional approaches.

title: Dynamic Quantum Error Correction Encoding and Topological Information Mapping
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic quantum error correction (QEC) scheme leveraging the principles of topological quantum systems. The core idea is to dynamically adapt the error correction strategy based on real-time analysis of the noise environment, eliminating the need for pre-encoded classical information. The scheme encodes error correction information into topological defects within topologically protected states, utilizing the inherent stability of these defects for robust error protection. Furthermore, a machine learning algorithm is integrated to continuously monitor the noise characteristics and optimize the correction parameters. The resulting approach offers enhanced correction efficiency compared to traditional static QEC methods, particularly in environments with evolving noise profiles. The primary theoretical contribution lies in decoupling the reliance on pre-encoded topological states for correction, paving the way for more adaptable and efficient quantum error correction. The proposed methodology aims to address a key limitation in current topological quantum computing architectures.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Topological Network
abstract: This paper proposes a novel architecture for a quantum network leveraging dynamic quantum entanglement and topological protection. The core claim is to construct a network capable of adaptive entanglement resource allocation and protection through the combination of coherent topological protection and dynamic entanglement routing. The key mechanism involves the exchange properties of coherent topological codes, quantum control-based entanglement routing protocols, and fault-tolerant entanglement encoding schemes, facilitating efficient quantum information transmission and robust protection within the topological network. The research addresses the limitations of existing topological quantum networks, which predominantly rely on static entanglement, by introducing a dynamic system with self-adaptive error correction and resource management. The system is designed to enhance the resilience and scalability of quantum networks for future quantum communication applications. The theoretical framework presented here provides a foundation for the development of practical dynamic quantum networks.

title: Title: Dynamic Parameter Adjustment Strategy for Non-Linear Self-Organizing Models
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic parameter adjustment strategy for non-linear self-organizing models. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often rely on static settings, potentially limiting model performance. This work proposes an algorithm that continuously monitors performance feedback and intelligently adjusts model parameters to optimize results. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that iteratively refines parameters based on observed outcomes, leading to improved model accuracy and robustness. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of simulations, showcasing significant performance gains compared to static parameter adjustments. The focus is on creating a model that adapts to changing data, offering a significant advancement in the field of self-organizing systems.

title: Adaptive Cognitive Architecture Simulation with Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to simulating human cognition by constructing an adaptive neural network architecture. The core claim is that a dynamically adjustable neural network structure and connections can more accurately model learning, memory, and decision-making processes inherent in human cognition. The proposed architecture, based on reinforcement learning, incorporates multiple modules – perception, memory, reasoning, and action – each with adaptive weight and connection adjustments driven by environmental feedback and internal simulations. A key element is the introduction of "concept units" to map abstract concepts to specific neural networks, enhancing expressive power. This adaptive framework addresses the limitations of traditional static cognitive architectures, offering a more nuanced and controllable model of complex cognitive dynamics. The simulation aims to provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition and potentially inform the development of intelligent systems.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing with Symbolic Representation Learning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to hyperdimensional computing (HDC) by integrating symbolic representation learning. Current HDC methodologies predominantly rely on vector representations, often overlooking the potential benefits of symbolic reasoning. We propose a framework that combines HDC with techniques like neural symbolic networks, allowing the system to learn and manipulate HDC vectors through symbolic logic. This integration aims to enhance the expressive power and interpretability of HDC systems. The core claim is that incorporating symbolic representation learning can significantly improve HDC's capabilities. We detail the proposed architecture, outlining the interaction between the vector-based HDC core and the symbolic reasoning layer. This work introduces a new paradigm for HDC, potentially leading to more robust and adaptable systems.

title: Protected-Code Recoverability as a Diagnostic for Spin-Coupled Gravitational Channels
abstract: Protected subspaces are usually introduced to suppress noise. Here they are used as diagnostic filters for gravitational channel structure. The question is not whether a gravitationally motivated environment causes decoherence, but what error algebra it induces on a protected code and its nearby error shell. We first formulate a recoverability diagnostic for collective versus constituent-resolving channels. For the code $\C=\operatorname{span}\{\ket{01},\ket{10}\}$, collective dephasing obeys $P_\C(Z_1+Z_2)P_\C=0$, while an unmatched spin-coupled response obeys $P_\C(q_1Z_1+q_2Z_2)P_\C=(q_1-q_2)Z_L$. Thus matched response is protected and unmatched response becomes logical dephasing. We then work this out in a weak-field axial-torsion model drawn from the propagating-torsion sector of quadratic Poincare gauge gravity. Under an even-$N$ CPMG sequence, the unmatched recoverability contrast samples a torsion spectral density at a tunable control frequency. A thermal or quasi-static axial background consistent with present spin-gravity and torsion bounds appears far too small for discovery, while a narrowband nonequilibrium bath remains only a conditional enhancement window. Finally, we describe three upgrade paths: $n>3$ hybrid-code design, a model-derived two-block axial exchange term, and a bath-commutator protocol. These are routes toward stronger nonclassicality tests, not results already achieved. The uploaded PDF contains the fully typeset abstract and mathematical notation.

title: Resource-adaptive distributed fault tolerance with very noisy Bell pairs
abstract: Distributed architectures have been proposed as a pathway to large-scale quantum computers. Combined with the need for fault-tolerance, such architectures require distributed quantum error correction (DQEC) and distributed logical gates. An important challenge is how to realize DQEC primitives in the setting where interaction between modules is restricted to shared Bell pairs that are significantly noisier than on-chip operations. We extend the framework known as fault tolerance by construction to this setting, deriving different strategies for handling the additional noise. Through fault-improvement we recover conventional entanglement distillation, and also find more dynamical protocols that enable space-time trade-offs. We show that integrated decoding halves the required distillation code distance compared to entanglement distillation implemented using separate decoding, thus requiring significantly fewer Bell pairs. As a main focus of the work, we synthesize efficient circuits for an important primitive in distributed fault tolerance: distributed stabilizer measurements. These circuits can be adapted to resource constraints, e.g. on the Bell pair generation rate or the space available for on-chip auxiliary qubits. Noting that full local fault-tolerance is not always needed to preserve the correct scaling of logical error rates, we further optimize the circuits depending on the surrounding context. We consider in particular the surface code and the color code, both as distributed memories and in the case of lattice surgery across separate modules. Here, robustness to certain hook and readout errors reduces the number of required Bell pairs even further, compared to the context-free setting. We numerically benchmark the resulting implementations under circuit level noise with additional interconnect noise.

title: PlantC2USeg: Cross-Scale Consistent Pre-Training for Few-Shot Unified Plant Point Cloud Segmentation
abstract: Modern crop breeding demands precise organ-level analysis for trait quantification, making plant point cloud segmentation (PPCS) increasingly important. However, conventional deep learning approaches rely heavily on densely annotated datasets that are labor-intensive to acquire. Unified PPCS adaptation from distribution-shifted examples with minimal additional training remains challenging. To address this, we propose PlantC2USeg, a deep transfer learning framework featuring cross-scale consistency learning to explicitly align features across spatial scales and an information-restricted decoding strategy that prevents reconstruction shortcuts and promotes robust adaptation. The resulting pre-training enables stable few-shot generalization across species and sensing conditions, while unified fine-tuning with inherited thresholds further reduces adaptation overhead. Under full supervision on Soybean3D, PlantC2USeg achieves the highest semantic IoU and instance mWCov among compared methods, at 91.91% and 94.62%. With 20 labeled samples, it leads both metrics at 89.78% and 90.27%; with only 10 samples, it retains the highest mWCov of 83.23% while achieving 83.19% IoU. Across HR3D, 10-shot transfer to tobacco, tomato, and sorghum averages 78.41% IoU and 79.42% mWCov, while 22-shot transfer to SYAU-Maize achieves the highest IoU and mRec at 92.75% and 93.51%. Furthermore, a leading category-averaged mIoU of 85.0% on ShapeNet Part demonstrates the framework's capability to handle diverse shape variations beyond agricultural domains. These results demonstrate that PlantC2USeg reduces overall adaptation effort under distribution shifts, enabling scalable plant phenotyping and transferable 3D representation learning beyond agriculture.

title: Conditional validity of quantum event classifiers under collider systematics and quantum estimation uncertainty
abstract: Claims about a deployed quantum machine-learning classifier can fail when target data shift or when finite-shot quantum evaluation randomizes the model itself. We develop an information-conditional, fail-closed auditing framework that returns supported, refuted or unresolved verdicts with anytime-valid per-claim error control under a declared sampling protocol. On a Higgs-to-tau-tau collider benchmark, stable classifier metrics do not guarantee valid signal-strength inference: at the studied finite-template statistics, the fixed-template profile can lose coverage, even in shift-free controls, when its templates are estimated independently and template-statistical uncertainty is not modeled explicitly. Across 30 frozen finite-shot quantum-kernel deployments, every realized Gram matrix is propagated through refitting, calibration and threshold selection; in the primary raw pipeline these perturbations leave ranking nearly unchanged yet move thresholded target metrics by about 0.02, flipping ideal-anchored claims, and the diagonal-loading sensitivity decomposes differently. Matched classical controls remove apparent quantum-specific nominal-performance and sensing effects. We claim no quantum advantage.

title: Evidence-Guided Detection, Localization and Explanation for Text-Centric Image Forensics
abstract: The rapid progress of AIGC has made text-centric image manipulation increasingly accessible, creating new forensic challenges that require not only authenticity detection but also spatial grounding and evidence-based explanation. This paper presents our solution to the GenText-Forensics Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026. We propose an evidence-guided detector-localizer-reasoner system, where an image-level detector provides a global authenticity prior, a dedicated localizer extracts tampered regions as spatial grounding evidence, and an MLLM-based reasoner generates structured forensic reports grounded in this expert forensic evidence. These modules are connected through a cascaded evidence flow: the detector gates the subsequent localization and prompting process, the localizer converts tamper responses into grounding boxes, and the reasoner is trained to synthesize the detector decision and localized evidence into the final report. As a key part of our method, we introduce iterative difficulty-aware mining to improve localization quality and apply report-mask consistency post-processing to align report grounding with predicted masks. On the official hidden test set, our system achieves a final score of 0.638 and ranks second in the challenge, validating the effectiveness of the proposed evidence-guided system. The code is available at https://github.com/peifengLiu42/ACMMM26-evidence-guided-detector-localizer-reasoner-system.

title: Five Dated Predictions on Meaning, Machines, and Human Thinking (2027–2032) — with Public Annual Review (v1.0)
abstract: Five dated, falsifiable predictions on meaning, machines, and human thinking (2027–2032), version 1.0, bilingual English/German — with a standing commitment to public annual review every September, beginning September 2027. Each prediction carries an explicit deadline and an explicit failure condition: (1) major agent-interoperability efforts adopt concept-level meaning-versioning by end-2028; (2) a recognized standards body publishes a specification for versioned, resolvable concept identifiers for AI systems by end-2030; (3) person-specific fidelity testing becomes an established evaluation category with at least three independent benchmarks by end-2030; (4) at least five organizations publicly report a human-capability measure alongside AI-productivity measures by end-2029; (5) a leading world-model system exposes an explicit, human-readable semantic interface by end-2032. Review rules are fixed in the document: wording frozen, failed predictions remain failed, public evidence only, and the author's own projects do not count as evidence for predictions 2, 3 and 5. The predictions extend theses the author has published openly (Universal Concept Layer; the Ehstand test; the semantic layer for world models). Licence note: CC BY-ND 4.0 covers the canonical text; trademark and name rights remain unaffected.

title: Quantum Topology Dynamic Adaptive Optimization
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field of physics, has recently emerged as a promising tool for computation and materials science. Its unique properties, such as the existence of stable, non-interacting quantum states, have implications for various areas, including quantum information theory and materials design. This paper explores the potential of quantum topology to revolutionize optimization, particularly in complex function optimization. We propose a novel dynamic adaptive optimization algorithm based on the principles of quantum topology, leveraging the inherent properties of topological structures to automatically adjust optimization parameters and achieve optimal solutions. This approach offers a significant advantage over traditional optimization methods, especially when dealing with complex, non-linear problems.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Random Matrix Generation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a peculiar phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for generating highly complex and statistically diverse random matrices. This paper explores the development of a novel random matrix generation algorithm leveraging quantum entanglement to produce matrices suitable for machine learning training and optimization. We detail the core mechanism, focusing on the instantaneous nature of entanglement and its application to matrix manipulation, demonstrating a potential paradigm shift in this field. Quantum entanglement offers a novel approach to randomness, potentially surpassing traditional methods in generating matrices with enhanced statistical properties.

title: RuFLEX: Hybrid Deep Fuzzy Learning Platform for Interpretable Model Engineering (Гибридная платформа глубокого нечёткого обучения для интерпретируемого моделирования)
abstract: RuFLEX v1.0.0 Первый публичный релиз RuFLEX — локальной научной платформы для проектирования, обучения, исследования и интерпретации нечётких, нейро-нечётких и классических моделей машинного обучения. Основные возможности проектирование Type-1 Mamdani и Sugeno FIS; настройка переменных, функций принадлежности, правил и нечётких операторов; обучение ANFIS и плоских нейро-нечётких моделей; поддержка глубокого нечёткого формирования признаков; сравнение с классическими моделями машинного обучения; многократные эксперименты с различными random seeds; разделение TRAIN / VALIDATION / CALIBRATION / TEST; калибровка вероятностей и выбор порогов по validation-данным; контролируемая финальная оценка на зафиксированной test-выборке; SHAP, TreeSHAP, Integrated Gradients, GradientSHAP и Occlusion; точные трассы выполнения нечётких систем и Decision Tree; анализ срезов данных и обобщающей способности моделей; контроль воспроизводимости объяснений; хранение происхождения данных, моделей, анализов и экспертных корректировок; формирование Verification Bundles и структурированных свидетельств результатов; импорт CSV/XLSX и совместимость с MATLAB .fis; графический интерфейс на React + TypeScript; FastAPI application layer; Python SDK для доступа к сохранённым объектам исследования. Архитектура RuFLEX использует объектно-ориентированную модель научного проекта, объединяющую: Data; Models; Studies; Analyses; Evidence. Результаты обучения, оценки, интерпретации и проверки сохраняются как связанные объекты проекта, что позволяет восстанавливать происхождение результатов и воспроизводить исследовательский процесс. Научное назначение RuFLEX предназначен для исследования гибридных нечётких и нейро-нечётких моделей с акцентом на интерпретируемость, воспроизводимость и контролируемую экспериментальную методологию. Платформа объединяет построение нечётких систем, обучение моделей, классические ML-бейзлайны, методы объяснимого искусственного интеллекта и средства формирования воспроизводимых исследовательских свидетельств в единой среде. Scientific safeguards RuFLEX разделяет этапы: TRAIN VALIDATION CALIBRATION TEST

Основные возможности проектирование Type-1 Mamdani и Sugeno FIS; настройка переменных, функций принадлежности, правил и нечётких операторов; обучение ANFIS и плоских нейро-нечётких моделей; поддержка глубокого нечёткого формирования признаков; сравнение с классическими моделями машинного обучения; многократные эксперименты с различными random seeds; разделение TRAIN / VALIDATION / CALIBRATION / TEST; калибровка вероятностей и выбор порогов по validation-данным; контролируемая финальная оценка на зафиксированной test-выборке; SHAP, TreeSHAP, Integrated Gradients, GradientSHAP и Occlusion; точные трассы выполнения нечётких систем и Decision Tree; анализ срезов данных и обобщающей способности моделей; контроль воспроизводимости объяснений; хранение происхождения данных, моделей, анализов и экспертных корректировок; формирование Verification Bundles и структурированных свидетельств результатов; импорт CSV/XLSX и совместимость с MATLAB .fis; графический интерфейс на React + TypeScript; FastAPI application layer; Python SDK для доступа к сохранённым объектам исследования. Архитектура RuFLEX использует объектно-ориентированную модель научного проекта, объединяющую: Data; Models; Studies; Analyses; Evidence. Результаты обучения, оценки, интерпретации и проверки сохраняются как связанные объекты проекта, что позволяет восстанавливать происхождение результатов и воспроизводить исследовательский процесс. Научное назначение RuFLEX предназначен для исследования гибридных нечётких и нейро-нечётких моделей с акцентом на интерпретируемость, воспроизводимость и контролируемую экспериментальную методологию. Платформа объединяет построение нечётких систем, обучение моделей, классические ML-бейзлайны, методы объяснимого искусственного интеллекта и средства формирования воспроизводимых исследовательских свидетельств в единой среде. Scientific safeguards RuFLEX разделяет этапы: TRAIN VALIDATION CALIBRATION TEST

title: 基于高维非线性图的自适应聚类算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel self-adaptive clustering algorithm designed for analyzing complex data. Traditional clustering methods often rely on manual feature design, limiting the algorithm's adaptability. We propose a new approach that leverages high-dimensional, non-linear graph representations to automatically adjust clustering parameters, enabling the algorithm to effectively identify patterns and structures within data. The core mechanism involves an adaptive learning algorithm that dynamically adjusts the parameters based on the data's inherent complexity, achieving robust and efficient clustering. This paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and performance evaluation, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing methods in identifying intricate data relationships and achieving accurate clustering. Keywords: Clustering, Self-Adaptive, Non-Linear Graph, Adaptive Learning, Data Analysis, Pattern Recognition Table of Contents

title: Probabilistic Programming for Automated Theorem Proving in Logic Programming
abstract: This paper explores the integration of probabilistic programming with logic programming to address the challenges inherent in automated theorem proving. Traditional automated theorem provers often struggle with incomplete knowledge, uncertain environments, and the need to explore a vast search space. We propose a novel approach where logic programs and proof strategies are modeled as probabilistic models. This allows the system to not only execute proof steps but also to assess the probability of success for each step, guiding the search process towards more promising paths. The core mechanism involves defining probability distributions over proof states, allowing the system to learn and adapt its strategy based on observed evidence. This work demonstrates the potential for creating a more robust, flexible, and ultimately, more effective automated theorem prover capable of handling complex logical problems with inherent uncertainty. The key contribution lies in the dynamic adjustment of proof strategies based on probabilistic assessments, moving beyond deterministic search algorithms. The formal framework presented here provides a foundation for future research in this area.

title: Information-Theoretic Regularization of Deep Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates a novel regularization technique for deep neural networks based on information-theoretic principles. The core idea is to mitigate overfitting, a common issue when training highly over-parameterized networks, by explicitly encouraging the network to maintain a high level of information flow between its layers. Traditional regularization methods, such as L1 and L2, implicitly constrain weights but do not directly address the quality of the learned representations. This approach introduces a regularization term derived from mutual information and entropy calculations, penalizing networks that excessively compress information. The methodology offers a principled means of controlling network complexity and promoting the learning of more robust and informative features, ultimately improving generalization performance. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the key equations and the optimization process. Empirical results (not presented experimentally here, but conceptually detailed) demonstrate the effectiveness of this information-theoretic regularization compared to conventional methods.

title: 基于自适应的自然语言处理的语法分析框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for grammatical analysis based on adaptive natural language processing (NLP) techniques. Traditional grammatical analysis relies heavily on manually crafted rules, limiting its flexibility and adaptability to the nuances of language. Our proposed system leverages self-adaptive algorithms to dynamically adjust grammatical rules based on sentence structure, offering a more robust and accurate analysis. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through a series of benchmark tests, showcasing significant improvements in precision and coverage compared to existing methods. The core mechanism focuses on a hierarchical rule adaptation process, allowing the system to effectively handle complex sentence structures and variations. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, including exploring the integration of contextual information and more sophisticated adaptive learning algorithms.

title: Causal Inference with Reverse Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to causal inference by integrating causal graph learning with reverse reinforcement learning (RRL). Traditional causal inference methods often struggle with uncertainty and rely on strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution. This research addresses this limitation by learning a probabilistic causal graph and then utilizing RRL to optimize policies within this graph, effectively navigating and mitigating the impact of uncertainty. The core claim is that this combined approach provides a more robust and reliable method for causal reasoning and decision-making. The paper details the methodology, focusing on the integration of causal inference techniques, such as structure learning and intervention learning, with the principles of RRL. The key mechanism involves constructing a probabilistic causal graph and applying RRL to refine strategies within it. This research demonstrates the potential to overcome the challenges associated with deterministic environments and provides a framework for more dependable causal inference in complex, uncertain systems. ---

title: Adaptive Learning Rate Dynamic Adjustment Strategy
abstract: This paper investigates and proposes a novel dynamic adjustment strategy for learning rates in machine learning models. Traditional learning rate scheduling methods often employ fixed or simplistic adaptive schemes that fail to adequately respond to the evolving dynamics of the training process. This can result in slow convergence, oscillations, and suboptimal solutions. The core claim of this work is that a dynamic adjustment strategy, informed by feedback from the training process – specifically gradient variations and loss function changes – can significantly improve both convergence speed and stability. We present a framework for building such a system, outlining the key components and considerations for effective implementation. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential to enhance training efficiency and robustness across a range of machine learning tasks. The key mathematical formulations are presented within this document.

title: Quantum State Modeling and Suppression of Quantum Decoherence
abstract: Quantum decoherence represents a significant obstacle to the advancement of quantum computing. This paper presents a novel approach to modeling and suppressing quantum decoherence, leveraging quantum control techniques. We establish a comprehensive mathematical model for quantum state decoherence, incorporating factors such as dephasing and dissipation. Subsequently, we develop a feedback control strategy based on real-time measurement of the quantum state, enabling precise suppression of decoherence. The core of our method relies on dynamically adjusting control pulses to counteract the detrimental effects of environmental interactions. Through theoretical analysis and mathematical formulation, we demonstrate the potential of this approach to significantly enhance the precision and stability of quantum computations. Our model incorporates key parameters including the initial state vector (ψ), the decoherence rate (γ), the dephasing rate (δ), the dissipation rate (κ), and the control pulse amplitude (F). The effectiveness of the control strategy is evaluated through simulations, showcasing a notable reduction in decoherence and improved fidelity of quantum operations. The proposed method offers a viable pathway towards building robust and scalable quantum computers.

title: Quantum Error Correction Protocols: A Topological Analysis of Non-Linearity
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a fundamental pillar of quantum computing, enabling reliable transmission and manipulation of quantum information. Traditional error correction methods rely on linear mathematical transformations, which are inherently limited in their ability to detect and correct errors. This paper explores the potential of using non-linear topological structures to fundamentally alter the design of quantum error correction protocols. We propose a novel framework that leverages these structures to enhance the robustness of QEC, potentially uncovering hidden physical laws governing the process. The core claim is that by analyzing quantum error correction protocols through a topological lens, we can identify crucial non-linearities and ultimately improve the protocol's effectiveness. This research aims to provide a new computational methodology for optimizing QEC, offering a path toward more reliable and scalable quantum systems.

title: 基于自适应网络结构的概率推理算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic reasoning algorithm based on an adaptive network structure. Traditional probabilistic reasoning often relies on static models, limiting flexibility and potentially hindering accurate reasoning under varying data. Our algorithm leverages the inherent self-adaptive properties of networks to dynamically adjust network structure and parameters, resulting in improved accuracy and adaptability. We explore the design of a mechanism that allows the network to adapt to changing data patterns, enhancing the algorithm's robustness and potential for handling complex probabilistic scenarios. This work addresses a key limitation of existing probabilistic methods, offering a more flexible and potentially superior approach to inference.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction Problem Solving with Hybrid Search
abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising approach to solving constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) due to its potential to escape local optima and explore the solution space more efficiently. However, traditional CSP solvers often struggle with highly complex, multi-variable problems. This paper investigates a novel hybrid search strategy that integrates quantum annealing with a modified CSP solver, leveraging quantum tunneling to accelerate the search process. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the speed and accuracy of solving complex CSPs compared to existing methods. The core mechanism involves combining quantum annealing with a dynamically adjusted CSP solver to effectively manage the high dimensionality of the problem. This work presents a new framework for tackling challenging CSPs with enhanced search capabilities.

title: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks for Synthetic Data Generation
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs) for the generation of synthetic data. Traditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) often face challenges in producing high-quality synthetic data, especially when dealing with complex data distributions. We propose a novel framework utilizing quantum circuits to construct both the generator and discriminator within a QGAN architecture. The core innovation lies in harnessing quantum superposition and interference during the adversarial training process to potentially improve the realism and diversity of the generated synthetic data. Our approach introduces a theoretical foundation and a conceptual design for QGANs, paving the way for future research and development in this emerging field. The primary goal is to demonstrate the potential benefits of incorporating quantum mechanical principles into the GAN framework, leading to enhanced synthetic data generation capabilities. The performance of a QGAN is expected to be superior to a classical GAN due to the unique properties of quantum systems.

title: Figure 5 from Counterfactual Diffusion Models Provide Interpretable Explanations of Artificial Intelligence Models in Pathology
abstract: Style–morphology decomposition for disentangling structural and staining effects on MSI prediction changes. A, Representative examples of counterfactual manipulation between MSIH and non-MSIH classes. For each original image x and its counterfactual xcf, style-hybrid (xstyle) and morphology-hybrid (xmorph) images were generated using Vahadane stain transfer. Each hybrid isolates the effect of either stain or morphology while controlling for the other. The right-hand bars show the Shapley-style decomposition of the logit change (Δf) into stain (φstyle) and morphology (φmorph) contributions, demonstrating that morphologic differences dominate the model’s predictions. Grad-CAM visualizations below provide region-level attribution under MIL. In contrast, MoPaDi produces class-directed “what-if” edits that offer a complementary view of candidate morphologic and style changes associated with prediction shifts. Scale bar applies to all images within the panel. B, Decomposition results across test-set patients, showing median contributions of φstyle, φmorph, and total (Δf) for manipulations toward (↑) and away from (↓) each class. C, Scatter plot of morphology versus style contributions per patient, illustrating consistent dominance of morphologic effects across both manipulation directions and classes.

title: Shuttling-aware dynamical decoupling for quantum charge-coupled devices
abstract: Dynamical decoupling (DD) helps maintain high-fidelity quantum computations by suppressing dephasing noise through carefully timed refocusing pulses. In quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures, however, where ions are shuttled throughout the device, transport constrains when pulses can be applied and affects the phase accumulated by an ion. Conventional DD methods do not account for shuttling and may therefore schedule pulses that must be omitted or shifted after transport scheduling, weakening the protection from dephasing. We therefore introduce shuttling-aware dynamical decoupling (SADD), an offline compiler pass that jointly selects refocusing pulses and local ion rerouting while preserving logical-gate timings and the total schedule length. In benchmark simulations, SADD improves average final-state fidelity over both the original schedules and a simple nearest-feasible Hahn-echo baseline when dephasing dominates control and transport errors and varies slowly enough for DD. Rerouting enables otherwise infeasible pulse timings, while spatial information about the noise can provide further gains. These benefits disappear, however, when the added transport introduces too much error. Overall, our results show that coordinating DD with ion transport is an effective compiler strategy for reducing dephasing in QCCD processors.

title: Unifying Function- and Argument-First Bidirectional Type Systems
abstract: Bidirectional typing mixes type synthesis and type checking into a single process. Existing bidirectional type systems can be classified into two styles based on whether, given a function application, a bidirectional typing algorithm synthesizes the function's type first and typechecks the argument against the synthesized argument type, or it synthesizes the arguments' types first and typechecks the function against the synthesized arguments' types. We call the former _function-first_ and the latter _argument-first_. Not only do the two styles significantly differ in how the type systems and typing algorithms are formalized, but also they lead to incompatible typeabilities, forcing a language designer to select one style and to give up the other's typeabilities. In this paper, we unify the two styles and develop \lang with a new bidirectional type system for higher-rank polymorphism. Key ideas of the unification are twofold. Each function application is annotated with a bit of information to represent whether function- or argument-first typing is used, to allow a language designer (or even a programmer) to switch between the two styles at their discretion. We reformulate the function- and argument-first type systems by using ideas from colored types and boxy types, which can specify which part of a type should be synthesized or used for checking in a flexible manner. We also develop a typing algorithm based on the worklist approach by Zhao et al. The (declarative) type system of $λ^{BH}$ is shown to be sound and to subsume two representative function- and argument-first systems. Our typing algorithm is shown to be sound with respect to the type system of $λ^{BH}$ and complete with respect to representative function- and argument-first systems. We mechanically prove the metatheorems using the Abella theorem prover.

title: Perfect transmission and parallel composition for quantum walks on graphs with two leads
abstract: Abstract We study scattering for continuous-time quantum walks on finite graphs with attached leads. The focus of our study is perfect transmission, which is essential for a given graph to be considered as a scattering gadget. To this end, we introduce three real parameters: the terminal-responses μ 1 and μ 2 , and a terminal-to-terminal coupling ν , defined in terms of characteristic polynomials of the graph and its vertex deleted subgraphs. Up to a momentum-dependent transformation, these quantities are the independent entries of an admittance matrix, and each is additive under parallel composition of graphs. In these variables the perfect transmission at a fixed momentum is characterized by a hyperbola in ( μ 1 , μ 2 , ν ) -space, the points of which determine the transmission phase. This turns the search for graphs with prescribed transmission properties into a geometric vector-sum problem for smaller building blocks.

title: Paying Too Much Attention? Why the Transformer vs. GBDT Debate is All About the Data
abstract: The current hype surrounding Transformer architectures has undeniably reached tabular machine learning. This paper investigates whether these novel models genuinely outperform traditional tree-based ensembles across all scenarios, or if enthusiasm obscures operational reality. A systematic benchmark comparing Deep Learning approaches (FT-Transformer, TabFlex, and the Foundation Model TabPFN) against established Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) is presented. Evaluating 20 diverse datasets under a strict fixed-budget protocol on consumer-grade hardware (Apple M1 Pro), the findings reveal that model superiority is strictly dictated by data scale, feature modality, and underlying inductive biases. While TabPFN excels in small-data regimes (N < 2,000) on continuous manifolds by leveraging pre-trained priors, tree-based ensembles consistently dominate larger datasets (N > 10,000) due to their axis-aligned decision boundaries and default robustness. Crucially, attention mechanisms incur training and inference latencies up to 1,000 times higher than GBDTs - a severe efficiency gap under Green AI considerations. Finally, interpretability trade-offs (TreeSHAP vs. opaque attention maps) and hybrid ensembling are integrated into a pragmatic practitioner's decision framework.

title: uuidna — content-addressed identity, honest by construction: 2499 distinct kernel-verified theorems under 2582 keys across 115 principles
abstract: A content-addressed identity system, honest by construction: a Lean 4 theorem ledger — 2499 distinct theorems under 2582 keys (a statement sealed in two wings is one theorem with two names), every one proven by decide, sorry-free, no Mathlib, axiom-free against the bare leanprover/lean4 kernel, folded to one order-invariant receipt (70b9fd4e-a4e7-8391-8281-c528ca72197e) — across 115 principles. Verified this era: the three-singularities theorem (only the digit 5 carries the mirror's fixed heart, the reflection's fixed digit, and the closure of both vortex rails); the forfeit law of the trial court (only a Lean-based proof is admissible and it wins the case — court_theorem_beats_assertion, court_loser_pays_the_two_coins, court_loser_develops_the_proven); the paper-on-trial wing (the published numbers of Nature DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10846-4 as decidable arithmetic, including the receipted refutation of the press's 'super-Eddington confirmed' by the paper's own 0.18, and the Balmer break derived from Rydberg arithmetic); the anti-fraud detector algebra; the involution census; and the legal due-process vocabulary. Also: holographic merkle proofs, a reversible imprint codec, the slim honesty gate (a fabricated citation is the one decidably-false case), pure-TypeScript ChaCha20-Poly1305 (KAT-pinned) under a 7-dimensional fold envelope, and an MCP server exposing the ledger. a content-address proves integrity, not truth; a verified theorem proves its exact statement, never a grander claim — verified is not solved, n=1 stays n=1, and every non-proven claim is remanded, not admitted. The proofs recompute from source with `npm run lean`; the deposited metadata is GENERATED from the ledger it describes, so the archive states the ledger that exists rather than one that has moved on.

title: De-identified analytic dataset for: Admission diagnosis text outperforms structured clinical variables in the early prediction of severe neonatal outcomes — a multi-task deep learning study of 11,377 NICU admissions
abstract: Release version of the analytic dataset underlying the article "Admission diagnosis text outperforms structured clinical variables in the early prediction of severe neonatal outcomes: a multi-task deep learning study of 11,377 NICU admissions" (manuscript under editorial consideration at Scientific Reports, 2026; no DOI has been issued). 11,377 neonatal intensive care admissions from three tertiary centres in China, admitted between 2020 and 2024, with 33 released fields: the 14 admission-available structured clinical features used by the models reported in the manuscript, the composite severity outcome and its two ascertainment criteria, six discharge-derived disease labels, length of stay and birth asphyxia, the analysis partition, and admission year and month. Direct identifiers, exact dates and all free-text clinical fields are withheld; the withheld fields and the reason for each are documented in withheld_fields.csv. Row order is randomly permuted and study identifiers carry no information about admission time. The package includes a data dictionary, a README recording the de-identification applied and the conditions of access, a SHA-256 manifest, and reproduce_release.py, which recomputes from the released file every quantity in the article that the released fields support and prints each against the value reported in the manuscript (64 of 66 checked quantities agree exactly; the two exceptions are the Table 1 cesarean-delivery row, for which a correction has been prepared to the publisher). Results that depend on the withheld admission diagnosis text, including the manuscript's primary model and its central comparison, cannot be reproduced from this file. Files are under restricted access: see README.md, section "Conditions of access", for who may request access and on what terms.

title: Nonlinear Topological Geometry Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on adaptive topological structure analysis. Traditional optimization methods often rely on simple search strategies, whereas this approach leverages the inherent advantages of topology to explore broader optimization spaces. The core mechanism involves real-time analysis of the model's topological structure, allowing for dynamic parameter adjustment to converge towards optimal solutions. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of illustrative examples, focusing on non-linear optimization problems.

title: Dynamic Topological Dependency Graph Learning and Program Generation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program synthesis that leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically learn and adapt the topological structure of dependency graphs, subsequently guiding the generation of program code. The core concept involves using reinforcement learning to optimize the dependencies between program modules, represented as a graph. The goal is to achieve more efficient and adaptable program synthesis. The system learns by receiving feedback from program execution (e.g., performance metrics, error rates) and adjusts the graph topology accordingly. A program generator then utilizes the learned dependency graph to produce code fragments, assembling them into complete programs. This closed-loop system addresses the limitations of traditional static dependency graph methods, particularly in complex and dynamic environments. The research focuses on creating a system capable of automatically discovering and refining the relationships between program components, leading to improved code quality and synthesis speed. The system's ability to learn and adapt in real-time represents a significant advancement in automated program synthesis techniques. ---

title: Quantum State Adaptive Geometry Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state adaptive geometry optimization algorithm designed to tackle high-dimensional optimization problems. We propose a quantum mechanism leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to explore the optimization landscape, enabling the discovery of global optima and efficient handling of complex scenarios. The core of our approach lies in the construction of a quantum state representation that effectively captures and manipulates the solution space, facilitating the exploration of the optimization function. This work demonstrates the potential of quantum optimization for a diverse range of problems, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to classical algorithms.

title: Adaptive Quantum Circuit Compilation based on Quantum Coherence Analysis
abstract: Quantum circuit compilation is a crucial step in transforming a high-level quantum algorithm description into a sequence of gates executable on a specific quantum hardware platform. Traditional compilation methods predominantly focus on minimizing gate count and circuit depth, often overlooking the significant impact of quantum coherence on the overall fidelity of the computation. This paper introduces an adaptive quantum circuit compilation algorithm designed to mitigate this limitation. The algorithm dynamically analyzes the coherence properties of the quantum circuit during the compilation process, aiming to preserve coherence while simultaneously minimizing detrimental decoherence effects. This approach represents a fundamental shift in the compilation paradigm, directly addressing the critical challenge of coherence maintenance in quantum computing. The proposed methodology utilizes a novel metric for coherence analysis and employs an adaptive optimization strategy to achieve superior circuit fidelity compared to conventional compilation techniques. The effectiveness of the algorithm is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of its components, paving the way for more robust and accurate quantum circuit implementations.

title: Dynamic Quantum Superposition: Adaptive Parameter Tuning for Enhanced Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for revolutionizing various fields, from drug discovery to materials science. However, the inherent complexity of quantum systems necessitates sophisticated control and manipulation techniques. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum computation, focusing on the dynamic adjustment of parameters within quantum superposition states. We introduce a new algorithmic framework, termed "Dynamic Quantum Superposition," that leverages the unique properties of dynamic quantum superposition to automatically adapt to the system's characteristics, enabling more flexible and efficient quantum computations. The core mechanism revolves around strategically manipulating the superposition state to achieve targeted computational outcomes. The proposed approach offers a significant advancement over existing quantum algorithms, specifically emphasizing parameter optimization and improved system-level modeling capabilities. This work presents a preliminary demonstration of the algorithm's efficacy through a simplified, yet illustrative, example, highlighting its potential for a future of enhanced quantum capabilities.

title: Quantum Chaos Computation: A Distributed Implementation
abstract: This paper explores the feasibility and potential of distributed quantum computation for simulating quantum chaos. The core claim is that leveraging distributed quantum systems can enable the parallel simulation of chaotic systems, thereby accelerating computationally intensive tasks. The proposed mechanism relies on harnessing the unique properties of quantum chaos – specifically, sensitivity to initial conditions – through quantum entanglement and coherence within a distributed network. We introduce a framework for constructing such a system and outline the key elements required for achieving this goal, including robust quantum communication protocols and algorithms designed to exploit the inherent parallelism. This approach addresses the limitations of single-quantum systems, offering a pathway to significantly enhanced computational power for applications such as complex system modeling, cryptography, and advanced materials simulation. The primary focus is on theoretical development, outlining the architecture and key considerations for a practical implementation. Further research is needed to develop specific algorithms and protocols optimized for distributed quantum chaos computation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Routing Protocol (QERP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Quantum Entanglement Routing Protocol (QERP), a novel approach to quantum communication designed to overcome the limitations of traditional single-photon transmission. QERP leverages multi-hop entanglement routing to establish a "quantum entanglement network," facilitating long-distance, high-bandwidth, and low-latency quantum information transfer. The core mechanism incorporates "entanglement enhancement" techniques to optimize entanglement quality and quantity, thereby increasing transmission range and channel capacity. This protocol addresses key challenges in quantum communication, namely coherence time decay and channel noise, providing a new paradigm for large-scale quantum networks. The theoretical framework presented here outlines the protocol's design and potential impact.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Routed Algorithms
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to network routing leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core claim is that quantum entanglement provides the potential for instantaneous information routing, surpassing the limitations imposed by classical communication channels. The proposed algorithm, a entanglement-based routing method, encodes data across multiple entangled quantum particles, exploiting the correlations inherent in entanglement to achieve instantaneous data transmission and routing within a network. This approach offers the possibility of drastically improved throughput and enhanced security compared to conventional routing protocols. The theoretical framework presented demonstrates the potential for a fundamentally new paradigm in network architecture and communication. Key parameters influencing performance are analyzed, including entanglement fidelity, number of entangled particles, and network topology. The ultimate goal is to establish a robust and scalable quantum routing system.

title: Fusion of String Theory and Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic potential of string theory and quantum machine learning, proposing a novel framework for advanced data analysis and physical modeling. We argue that harnessing the unique properties of string theory, particularly its representation of quantum states, can significantly enhance the capabilities of quantum machine learning algorithms. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum states within string theory models to train quantum machine learning algorithms, leading to a deeper understanding of complex physical phenomena and facilitating the development of a new generation of predictive models. This work presents a conceptual framework and preliminary results demonstrating the potential for this integration, highlighting key challenges and opportunities for future research.

title: Adversarially Robust QSL on UNSW-NB15 experiment
abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility package for a controlled study of adversarial robustness in quantum supervised learning (QSL) for network intrusion detection using the UNSW-NB15 benchmark. The experiment evaluates a four-qubit variational QSL intrusion detector together with a matched classical multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline. The shared preprocessing pipeline applies categorical encoding, feature extraction, principal component analysis to four dimensions, and scaling to the interval [0, π]. Experiments are conducted over ten matched random seeds. White-box Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks are evaluated at perturbation budgets ε/π = 0.02, 0.05, and 0.10. The robust QSL training protocol uses a mixture of 50% clean, 25% FGSM, and 25% PGD samples. PGD uses three steps during adversarial training and seven steps during final evaluation. The repository contains the principal experiment notebooks, repeated-seed robustness results, attack diagnostics, statistical summaries, confidence intervals, paired statistical tests, effect-size analyses, and quantum-versus-classical comparison outputs. Across ten matched seeds, PGD-aware adversarial training improves QSL accuracy from 9.10% to 26.90% under PGD at ε = 0.05π and from 2.60% to 20.73% at ε = 0.10π. This improvement is accompanied by a reduction in clean QSL accuracy from 70.73% to 61.57%. The adversarially trained classical MLP retains higher absolute robustness, achieving 64.27% and 50.50% accuracy at PGD 0.05π and 0.10π, respectively. These results demonstrate that PGD-aware adversarial training materially strengthens the evaluated QSL model but do not establish quantum advantage. The repository is intended to support transparent reproduction, independent verification, and further research on adversarial robustness in quantum machine learning for cybersecurity.

title: Title: Dynamic Probabilistic Graphs via High-Dimensional Neural Networks: Semantic Reasoning and Knowledge Graph Construction in Natural Language Processing
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic probabilistic graph model, leveraging high-dimensional neural networks, for natural language processing. We propose a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the network parameters to enhance both semantic reasoning and knowledge graph construction capabilities. The core challenge lies in developing a model capable of learning complex language representations and effectively constructing knowledge graphs, which are crucial for many NLP tasks. The study investigates the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experimentation on various semantic reasoning and knowledge graph tasks. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in these tasks, highlighting the potential of this dynamic probabilistic graph model as a foundation for advanced NLP applications.

title: Dynamic Code Synthesis of Symbolic Program Generation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program synthesis, termed Dynamic Code Synthesis (DCS), which aims to generate optimized program code dynamically based on input data and a specified objective function. Unlike traditional static program synthesis methods that produce fixed programs, DCS employs symbolic program generation techniques combined with runtime optimization algorithms. The core mechanism involves symbolic reasoning and iterative code refinement to produce code that directly addresses the given constraints and maximizes the desired performance. This work demonstrates the feasibility and potential of DCS, offering a pathway towards truly adaptive and self-optimizing software systems. The system achieves this by dynamically creating and modifying programs in a symbolic space, guided by the input data and the objective function, resulting in code that is tailored to specific scenarios. The system utilizes a combination of techniques, including constraint solving, program transformation, and evolutionary algorithms, to achieve this dynamic synthesis. The research presented here contributes to the field of automated program synthesis by introducing a new paradigm that allows for the creation of programs that can adapt and improve themselves over time. The primary goal is to create a system that can generate code that is not only correct but also performs optimally, even in situations where the initial design is incomplete or inaccurate.

title: Gradient-Free Optimization for Matrix functions
abstract: We consider the task of optimizing smooth, possibly non-convex functions of a matrix variable given access only to directional derivatives rather than full gradients. This setting arises when fine-tuning large neural networks on consumer-grade hardware: the network's weights are matrices, memory constraints rule out backward-mode automatic differentiation, but directional derivatives remain available through forward mode. We frame gradient estimation in this setting as a structured recovery problem, in the spirit of signal processing. From this perspective we provide three contributions. First, we introduce an alternative to the standard random gradient estimator; the difference corresponds to replacing the adjoint of the sampling operator with its pseudoinverse. Second, when the gradient satisfies an approximate low-rank condition, techniques from matrix sensing yield a family of highly accurate gradient estimators that drop into any first-order method. Third, we note that while the computational cost of such estimators is high, this can be amortized by combining them with a matrix-aware optimizer such as spectral descent. Specifically, the gradient estimator computes a factorization of the gradient, allowing for the projection step of spectral descent to be done at no extra cost. We demonstrate our findings with two careful numerical experiments on synthetic functions with approximately low-rank gradients. We show that by exploiting this low-rank property one obtains much faster convergence to good approximate solutions.

title: ProbeMatchDTI: Probe-Driven Multi-Scale Biochemical Pattern Matching for Drug-Target Interaction Prediction
abstract: Drug-target interaction (DTI) prediction is an important task in AI-driven drug discovery. Although recent biochemical representation learning methods have improved DTI prediction, their passive feature aggregation tends to favor dominant molecular patterns while suppressing weak yet binding-relevant signals, such as functional groups and residue-context patterns, limiting the modeling of multi-scale biochemical correspondences. To address this issue, we propose ProbeMatchDTI, a pattern-probe-driven framework comprising IterProbe and BindingProbe. IterProbe explicitly retains contextual states across refinement depths and uses learnable probes to select them at each position before cross-entity matching, thereby preserving weak biochemical patterns and strengthening associations among functional groups, local motifs, and molecular scaffolds. BindingProbe then characterizes cross-entity drug-protein complementarity at local biochemical-unit and whole-pair levels, jointly modeling fine-grained interactions and multi-scale correspondences while preserving weaker binding-relevant associations. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of ProbeMatchDTI, achieving 2.0% and 0.5% higher AUC-ROC on BindingDB and DrugBank, respectively. Feature-level pattern analyses further characterize its probe-driven behavior in cross-scale biochemical pattern matching. We further connect ProbeMatchDTI predictions with an evidence-guided downstream drug-discovery workflow, demonstrating their utility for candidate refinement and validation planning. Our code is available at https://github.com/developer-hq/ProbeMatchDTI

title: READY or Not: Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment
abstract: An AI agent can perform well on benchmarks and still be unsuitable for deployment. Existing AI-agent benchmarks measure whether an agent can complete realistic professional work, whereas enterprise deployment asks a different question: whether an agent can meet a required reliability level, under acceptable human oversight, and at tolerable cost. We introduce Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment (READY), a framework for qualifying AI agents for deployment on enterprise workflows. READY preserves each workflow's own definition of successful execution while applying a common qualification procedure. Given an agent, a workflow, and a class of candidate oversight policies, READY measures the reliability and operating cost of the human-AI system, selects the minimum-cost policy that satisfies a specified reliability target, and statistically qualifies it on held-out cases. The resulting deployment profile characterizes the supported operating point: reliability, human-oversight burden, and cost. READY is implemented as an open testbed that decouples workflow specification, execution, evaluation, and qualification, and runs on existing agent-evaluation infrastructure. In an end-to-end clinical-audit case study spanning 16 agent systems and 750 cases, READY reveals differences hidden by autonomous performance: two systems separated by only 0.3 points in autonomous accuracy (72.8% vs. 72.5%) require 39.2% versus 29.6% human review, respectively, to qualify at the same 76% reliability target under the evaluated oversight policy. READY thus shifts enterprise agent evaluation from how well can the agent perform the work? to under what conditions, and at what cost, can it be reliably deployed? By making those conditions explicit and statistically testable, READY provides a basis for comparing agent systems, setting oversight requirements, and making evidence-based deployment decisions.
